scenes.narration: Your server is down. The fix is one command. You just can't remember which one.
That's the gap this video closes. Every command a Linux sysadmin actually types, all hundred and nine, each one running on screen. Welcome to THE NBX STUDIO.
Here's how we'll keep a hundred and nine of anything straight. Your terminal is a workbench, every command is a tool, and the tools live in ten drawers.

toolBench.headline: One bench, [ten drawers]
toolBench.caption: Learn the drawers, not the list.

scenes.narration: One warning first. Somewhere in these hundred and nine sits a command that wipes an entire disk in four characters. No prompt, nothing in a bin. So which one is it? We'll get there.

reveal.statement: One of them wipes a disk in four characters.

scenes.narration: We'll work through the drawers in order. Files and the text inside them. Then who's allowed to touch what. Then the processes running right now, and how you watch a machine properly. Then disks and the network. And finally the jobs and sessions that outlive you closing the laptop.
Drawer one. Moving around, and handling files.

Your project lives a few folders deep and you want to work inside it. The command is C D, short for change directory. One way in is an absolute path, which begins at the root slash, and the shell walks down it a level at a time: the root of the disk, into home, where every user's folder lives, into dev, your own account, and finally into api. The other way is a relative path, which begins wherever you're standing. To reach the logs folder beside you, type C D dot dot slash logs, where two dots mean up one level, and you drop into logs. None of those folders moved. Only where you're standing changed. So a path is just directions to a place which was already there, and cd walks them for you.

cmdCd.headline: cd moves [you], not the files
cmdCd.verdictSub: only your position in the tree did

scenes.narration: Here's something which happens more often than people admit. You've been jumping between folders and you genuinely can't remember which one you're sitting in. The command which answers is P W D, which stands for print working directory. P W D replies with the whole path, read top down: the root of the disk, then home, which holds every user's folder, then dev, your own account, and finally api, where you're standing. Joined up, that's the full path. And it's the same answer no matter where you started from, because P W D will never hand you a relative path, and never a shortcut either. P W D answers from the root every single time. When a script needs to know where it is, pwd is the answer it can rely on.

cmdPwd.headline: pwd prints [where you stand]
cmdPwd.verdict: It answers from the root, every time
cmdPwd.verdictSub: which is exactly why scripts can trust it

scenes.narration: You want to see what's inside a folder. L S, short for list, gives you the names and nothing else, which is fine until you need detail. Add the dash L flag for long and you get L S dash L, where every file becomes a full row. That row carries the permissions, saying who may read, write and run it, the owner, the account it belongs to, the size in bytes, and the date it last changed. Those raw byte counts are hard to read, so add an H for human and you get L S dash L H, which turns four thousand and ninety six into a plain four kilobytes. Same directory each time. You're just asking for more of the truth. Reach for ls dash L H by default, because the extra columns cost you nothing.

cmdLs.headline: ls shows names. [ls -l] shows the truth

steps.label: ls -l
steps.detail: one row per file, seven columns

stage.label: size
stage.sub: in bytes, until you ask otherwise

cmdLs.verdict: Same directory, three levels of detail
cmdLs.verdictSub: ls -lh is the one worth putting in muscle memory

scenes.narration: You need a new folder, so you reach for make dir, short for make directory. Inside projects, which already exists, it drops api into place without fuss. Now try asking for a path three levels deep in a single command, and it refuses outright. Make dir only ever creates the last folder in a path, and here the middle level doesn't exist, so make dir has nowhere to put the bottom one. The fix is the dash P flag, short for parents, so you type make dir dash P and make dir builds every level that's missing: src appears inside api, and then handlers appears inside src. Without dash P the parent has to exist first. Type mkdir dash P out of habit and you'll never meet that error again.

cmdMkdir.headline: mkdir -p builds the [whole chain]
cmdMkdir.verdict: Without -p, the parent must already exist
cmdMkdir.verdictSub: which is the entire reason the plain form failed

scenes.narration: Touch looks like a command which does nothing at all, which is exactly why people skip straight past it. Start with a name that doesn't exist yet. Run touch on it and Linux creates an empty file for you, zero bytes, no contents whatsoever. So far, so unremarkable. Now run touch on that same file a second time. The contents don't change, because there are none, but two clocks attached to that file do move: the modify time, which records when the contents last changed, and the access time, which records when it was last read. And build tools watch those clocks. The content itself is never touched. Touch exists to move a clock forward, and which turns out to be worth a whole command.

cmdTouch.headline: touch sets [timestamps], not content

steps.label: touch notes.md
steps.detail: file existed — only the clock moved

steps.label: touch notes.md
steps.detail: file existed — only the clock moved

stage.label: run it again
stage.sub: on the file that now exists

cmdTouch.verdictSub: which is exactly why make and every build tool relies on it

scenes.narration: C P, which is short for copy, makes a genuine second copy of a file. So the original stays exactly where it was, and a second file comes into existence holding its own bytes. If what you want is a whole folder and everything inside it, add the dash R flag, short for recursive, and C P dash R walks the directory so that every file underneath is copied as well. Here's the part which matters. You now have two independent files that merely happen to hold the same contents. Edit the original and the copy doesn't follow, because nothing connects them. That seems obvious until the afternoon you edit the backup by mistake. Copy when you want two things. Move when you want one thing somewhere else.

cmdCp.headline: cp makes a [second file]

stage.label: backup.md
stage.sub: a second, real set of bytes

stage.label: -r, for recursive
stage.sub: when it is a whole folder

cmdCp.verdict: Two separate files from the moment it runs

scenes.narration: M V is short for move, and it's also how you rename things, because renaming really is just moving a file to a new name in the same folder. The trick is to watch the file rather than the name on it. You start with notes dot M D, and underneath, the disk knows it by a number called an inode. Rename it and you get a new name sitting on the very same inode. Now move it into another folder and the path changes while that inode stays exactly as it was. No second copy was created, and not one byte was rewritten. The one exception is moving between two disks, and then the bytes really do travel. Inside one filesystem, nothing is copied. That's also why moving a file to another disk takes time when renaming it never does.

cmdMv.headline: mv renames and moves — [same command]

stage.label: inode 4812
stage.sub: the file the disk actually knows

cmdMv.verdict: No copy is made inside one filesystem
cmdMv.verdictSub: which is why moving a huge file is instant

scenes.narration: R M is short for remove, and the first thing to understand is that Linux has no recycle bin waiting to catch your mistake. Point plain R M at a folder and R M refuses, because on its own it only deletes files. Add dash I for interactive and R M dash I asks you to confirm every single file before it goes, which is slow but survivable. The combination people actually type, though, is dash R F, meaning recursive and force. Run R M dash R F and it recurses into every folder underneath while force suppresses every question it'd have asked. Four hundred and twelve files, gone, without one confirmation. There's no undo here, and no command that brings them back. Type the path out in full before you press return, every single time.

cmdRm.headline: Every guard on [rm] is opt-in

steps.label: rm -rf projects
steps.detail: no prompt, no bin, no undo

cmdRm.verdictSub: the only real protection is a backup you made earlier

scenes.narration: L N, short for link, gives one file a second name. To see why which matters, look at the data itself, sitting in one place on the disk. A plain L N creates a hard link, a second name pointing straight at that data, and the link count, which counts the names attached, goes up to two. Now add dash S for symbolic and L N dash S makes something quite different: a link which points at the name rather than at the data. The difference stays invisible until you delete the original name. The hard link carries on working perfectly, because the data was never tied to that first name. The symbolic one is now pointing at nothing. The data survives until the last name goes. Use a hard link for a second real name, and a symlink when you want a pointer.

cmdLn.headline: A hard link is a [second name]

stage.label: backup.md
stage.sub: a hard link, straight to the data

stage.label: latest.md
stage.sub: a symbolic link, pointing at the name

stage.label: backup.md still works
stage.sub: the data was never tied to that name

stage.label: latest.md dangles
stage.sub: the name it pointed at is gone

cmdLn.verdictSub: the data lives until the very last name goes

scenes.narration: Your terminal has turned into an unreadable mess, so you run clear. The screen was full of output, and above it sat the scrollback, everything that had already scrolled off the top. After clear the screen looks empty, which is genuinely useful. But look at the scrollback, because it's entirely intact. Scroll up and every line you thought you removed is still there. If you want it properly gone, reset is the heavier tool, and after reset the scrollback goes as well. Clear is cosmetic and reset is not, which matters on a machine somebody else can scroll back through. On somebody else's machine, assume clear removed nothing at all.

cmdClear.headline: clear hides. [reset] forgets

stage.label: scroll up
stage.sub: and it is all still there

cmdClear.verdict: clear is cosmetic, reset is not
cmdClear.verdictSub: which matters on a machine somebody else can scroll back through

scenes.narration: Quick check. You delete the original file. Which link still works? Have a think, and pause here if you want longer. Ready? The hard link, because it points at the data.

quiz.question: Delete the original — which link still works?
quiz.why: A hard link points at the data, not at the name.

scenes.narration: Drawer one is your hands. Move with C D, look with L S. Build with make dir and touch. Duplicate with C P, rename with M V. Delete with R M, because there's no undo.

points.text: cd and ls to move and look

scenes.narration: Drawer two. Reading text, and finding it, because most of the job is reading.

Cat is short for concatenate, and its actual job is to print a file straight to your screen. Point it at a small config file, three lines long, and you get the whole thing at once, which is exactly right. Now take a log file with ten thousand lines in it and run cat on that instead. Cat does exactly the same thing, because printing everything is the only behaviour it has. The output scrolls past far faster than you can read, there's no way to pause it, and no way to scroll back to the top. Cat has no brakes, and that's precisely what less was written for. Use cat for a config file you can see all of, and less for anything bigger.

cmdCat.headline: cat prints [everything], instantly

stage.label: all of it, at once
stage.sub: and it fits on the screen

cmdCat.verdictSub: which is precisely what less was written for

scenes.narration: Cat prints a file from the top down, so you get line one, then line two, then line three, oldest first. That's the wrong way round for a log, where the line you care about is nearly always the last one written. Somebody noticed, and named the fix by spelling cat backwards. That tool is tac, and tac reads the file from the bottom upwards. So the crash at nine forty seven arrives first, and the startup message from nine o'clock comes last. And the file itself is untouched; only the output order changed. No flags, no pipe, no arguments. In most logs the line you want is the final one. Tac is a one-word change from cat, and on a log it saves you a scroll every time.

cmdTac.headline: tac is cat, [backwards]

stage.label: now reversed
stage.sub: the file is read bottom up

cmdTac.verdict: Newest first, and no flags needed
cmdTac.verdictSub: in most logs the line you want is the last one

scenes.narration: Before less existed this was the tool everybody used, and it's still on every machine you'll ever log into. You point more at a file far longer than your screen, and more hands you the first forty lines or so. Press the space bar and it moves you down to the next forty. That much is genuinely useful. But now try to go back to something you just read, and you simply cannot, because more only ever travels forwards. Not even one line back. And once you reach the bottom it quits on you. And which is why less replaced it. One direction, then it exits, which is the frustration less was built to fix. You'll still meet more on a stripped-down system, so it's worth knowing why it annoys you.

cmdMore.headline: more only goes [forward]
cmdMore.verdict: One direction only, then it exits
cmdMore.verdictSub: which is the whole reason less exists

scenes.narration: Less does everything more did, and then fixes what more got wrong. You can scroll down a page at a time, and crucially you can scroll back up, which more could never manage. Then there's the part which genuinely surprises people. Open a ten gigabyte log with less and it appears on screen instantly, because it never loads the whole file into memory; it reads only the piece you're looking at. And when you know roughly what you're hunting for, press slash to search inside the file and it'll jump straight to the match. Which is why file size stops mattering. Less is the reader you should reach for by default, whatever the size of the file.

cmdLess.headline: less goes [both ways]

stage.label: it never loads it all
stage.sub: only the part you are reading

cmdLess.verdictSub: which is why file size stops mattering at all

scenes.narration: In a log of thousands of lines, the ones you want sit at the bottom. Tail gives you exactly that: the last twenty lines, nothing above them. That alone saves a lot of scrolling, and most of the time it's all you need. But the flag which genuinely matters here's dash F, for follow. Run tail dash F and the file is held open, so new lines appear as the service writes them. A request comes in live. Then another. And then the upstream timeout you were waiting for. Tail never exits on its own; control C is how you let it go. Tail is the command you leave running while you reproduce the bug. Two windows, tail dash F in one of them, and the bug tells you about itself.

cmdTail.headline: tail -f watches it [happen]

stage.label: upstream timeout
stage.sub: the line you were waiting for

stage.label: Ctrl-C
stage.sub: is how you let it go

cmdTail.verdict: This is the one you leave running
cmdTail.verdictSub: a bug you can watch happen is a bug you can fix

scenes.narration: V I traps more beginners than any other command on this list, and the reason is modes. When it opens you're in command mode, which means the keys are instructions rather than letters. Press J and you move down; you don't type a J. Which is why typing your name appears to do nothing sensible. Press I, which stands for insert, and those very same keys now produce text on the page. When you're done, press Escape and they turn straight back into commands. To save and leave, type a colon, then W to write the file, then Q to quit the editor. Escape, colon, W, Q. Memorise that one sequence and V I stops being frightening. And if you ever land in vi by accident, that same sequence is how you get out.

cmdVi.headline: vi has [two modes]
cmdVi.verdictSub: the one sequence worth memorising on day one

scenes.narration: You've two config files which are almost identical, and something in one of them has broken the service. Rather than read both and trust your eyes, run diff, which walks both files line by line at the same moment. Everything that matches is dimmed away, and nothing else is mentioned at all. What's left is the pair which genuinely differs: the old listen line on port eighty, marked as removed, and the new one on four four three, marked as added. Two entire files reduced to two lines. Add dash U for the unified format. That's what every patch you've ever applied is written in. Before you edit any config on a live server, diff it against the one that worked.

cmdDiff.headline: diff shows [only the change]
cmdDiff.verdict: It shows you only what moved
cmdDiff.verdictSub: and diff -u is the format every patch is written in

scenes.narration: Find does exactly what the name says, and find does it the hard way. Find walks the entire tree beneath wherever you point it, folder by folder, testing every file against your conditions. Ask it for anything ending in dot log and api dot log matches, while notes dot M D is rejected because it's not a log. Conditions stack, so add dash M time minus two and you're now also asking for files changed in the last two days. Web dot log is two hours old and stays, but old dot log is ninety days old and drops out. There's no index behind this. Find is slow because find genuinely looks. When correctness matters more than speed, find is the tool which will not lie to you.

cmdFind.headline: find [tests] every single file

stage.label: notes.md
stage.sub: is not a log at all

stage.label: -mtime -2
stage.sub: changed in the last two days

cmdFind.verdict: Slow, because it really does look
cmdFind.verdictSub: which is also why the answer is always current

scenes.narration: Locate answers the same question as find, but in a fraction of a second, and the reason is worth knowing. Somewhere on your machine sits a database of filenames, rebuilt in the small hours. Locate never touches your disk at all; it only searches that database. So a file you made last week is in the index and comes back instantly, with no walking at all. But ask it for a file you created at eight this morning and you get nothing, because the index hasn't been rebuilt since three. Running updatedb rebuilds it on demand. Locate can be fast and wrong at the same time, so use find when it has to be current. Reach for locate when you're guessing, and find when you need to be certain.

cmdLocate.headline: locate is fast, and can be [wrong]

stage.label: notes.md
stage.sub: made last week, and in the index

cmdLocate.verdictSub: or use find whenever the answer has to be current

scenes.narration: Grep searches inside files and prints every line containing what you asked for, which makes it the single most used tool on this list. The name comes from an old editor command, global regular expression print. A few flags carry most of the weight. Dash I ignores case, so timeout and Timeout both match. Dash R searches whole directories rather than one file. Dash C, for count, gives you just the number of matching lines instead of the lines themselves. And dash V, for invert, returns everything that doesn't match. That last one hides the noise. Dash V is the flag people forget they have. Grep is the tool you'll type more than any other, so the flags repay learning properly.

cmdGrep.headline: grep finds the [matching lines]
cmdGrep.verdict: -v is the flag people forget they own

scenes.narration: Awk is named after the three people who wrote it, and awk exists to pull columns out of text. Take one line of output. Awk splits it on whitespace automatically, without you writing a single line of parsing code, and numbers the pieces. Dollar one is the filesystem, dollar two is the total size, dollar three is the amount used. So asking for dollar three pulls that column out of every row at once. And because awk runs your snippet on each line in turn, you can keep a running total and add the column up as it goes past. Which is why awk beats writing a parser for a one-off question. Any time you catch yourself about to write a script to read columns, try awk first.

cmdAwk.headline: awk splits a line into [fields]

stage.label: one line of output
stage.sub: before anything is done to it

cmdAwk.verdictSub: whitespace does the splitting for you

scenes.narration: Sed is short for stream editor, and sed edits text as that text flows past it. A line goes in, the pattern you gave it matches somewhere inside, and the altered line comes out the other side. There's a catch that bites everybody once: by default it changes only the first match on each line. Add a G on the end, for global, and it changes every one. And here's the bigger catch. Everything you've just watched printed to the screen, but the file on disk was never modified at all. Add dash I, for in place, and now it genuinely is edited. Without dash I, sed only ever prints. Run it without dash I once, read the output, then run it again with dash I.

cmdSed.headline: sed edits the [stream]

stage.label: nothing was saved
stage.sub: the file on disk is untouched

cmdSed.verdictSub: which is a mercy the first few times you use it

scenes.narration: Here's a pipeline which looks completely reasonable and quietly does nothing at all. Find prints its filenames down the pipe, exactly as you'd expect. But R M doesn't read from a pipe. Xargs reads arguments, the words you type after the command. So the names arrive, nothing is listening, and not a single file is deleted, with no error to tell you. Xargs is the adapter that fixes it. Xargs sits in the middle, reads the incoming names, and hands them to R M as arguments instead, so the delete finally runs. If your filenames contain spaces, use dash print zero with dash zero. Whenever a pipe seems to do nothing at all, xargs is usually the missing piece.

cmdXargs.headline: xargs turns input into [arguments]

stage.label: xargs sits in between
stage.sub: and converts one into the other

cmdXargs.verdictSub: a filename with a space breaks the simple form

scenes.narration: Quick one. You want every line which does not contain the word error. Which grep flag? Have a think, and pause here if you need longer. Ready? Dash V, because dash V inverts the match.

quiz.question: Every line WITHOUT "error" — which flag?
quiz.why: -v inverts the match, printing what does not match.

scenes.narration: Drawer two is your eyes. Cat and less read, tail follows. Find walks the disk, locate guesses. Grep, awk and sed search and rewrite. Xargs joins them, which is why pipes work.

points.text: grep, awk, sed to search and edit

scenes.narration: Drawer three. Who you are, and what you're allowed to touch.

Change mod, spelled C H M O D, is short for change mode, and a file's mode is really just nine switches. They come in three banks of three. The first bank is the owner, the account the file belongs to. The second is the group, meaning everybody in the file's group. The third is other, which is literally everyone else. Each bank has read worth four, write worth two, and execute worth one, so seven is four plus two plus one, all three switches on, while five is four plus one, read and execute with the write left off. If numbers don't suit you, the letter form sets exactly the same nine switches. Seven is all three. Five drops the write. Read any permission string in threes and the number stops being something you memorise.

cmdChmod.headline: chmod flips [nine switches]

stage.label: owner
stage.sub: the account that owns the file

cmdChmod.verdict: 7 is all three, 5 drops the write
cmdChmod.verdictSub: that is the whole of what 755 means

scenes.narration: Change own, spelled C H O W N, is short for change owner, and change own hands a file to somebody else. This file belonged to dev, and after running that one short command it belongs to the deploy account instead. Files carry a group as well as an owner, and very often you want to set the two of them together in one go. So add a colon and a second name, and you set both at once, making the group W W W. Now look carefully at what didn't happen. The nine permission switches haven't moved a millimetre. Read, write and execute are set exactly as they were before. What changed is that the first bank now describes a different person. Permissions describe a role rather than a person, which is precisely why these are two separate commands. So when a service can't read its own config, check the owner before you change the mode. Change the mode when the rules are wrong; change the owner when the person is.

cmdChown.headline: chown hands the file [to someone]

stage.label: now it is deploy
stage.sub: the same file, a new owner

stage.label: add a colon
stage.sub: and you set the group too

cmdChown.verdictSub: only the people they point at did

scenes.narration: Here's a question almost nobody asks. When you make a new file, where do its permissions actually come from? The answer is U mask, short for user file creation mask. Every new file starts life at six six six, read and write for everyone. Your mask, typically zero two two, lists the bits you never want handed out, and those switches are simply subtracted. What survives is six four four, which is exactly what you get when you create a fresh file. Directories are slightly different: they start at seven seven seven, because you need execute permission to enter one at all, so the same mask leaves them at seven five five. And note that a mask never adds a single bit; it can only remove them, which is exactly what the word mask means. U mask can only take away. You'll rarely change your umask, but knowing it exists explains every new file you make. Run umask once on a machine you administer, and every new file afterwards makes sense.

cmdUmask.headline: umask decides what [new files] get

stage.sub: what you actually end up with

stage.label: directories start at 777
stage.sub: not 666, because you must enter them

stage.label: the same mask gives 755
stage.sub: which is why folders look different

cmdUmask.verdictSub: a mask can only ever take permissions away

scenes.narration: Restarting a service is something only an administrator may do, so run it as yourself and you get permission denied, which is the system working as intended. The obvious fix is to log in as root, and it's the wrong one, because then every command carries full power and nothing records who you were. What you want is to borrow that power once. So put sudo in front, short for superuser do. First a rule file called sudoers is consulted to answer one question: is this user allowed to run this particular command? If the answer is yes, the command runs with full root privilege, and a line goes into the audit log naming you. And then the privilege is handed straight back, so the next thing you type runs as you again. Sudo lasted exactly one command, and that's the entire point. Use sudo for the command that needs it; staying yourself is the safer default.

cmdSudo.headline: sudo lends power for [one command]
cmdSudo.verdictSub: the privilege lasts exactly one command

scenes.narration: User add looks like one small command, and it's quietly doing four things at once. User add writes a line into etc passwd, which is the account itself. User add writes an entry into etc shadow, where the password hash will eventually live. User add creates a group with the same name as the user. And then it stops, because the home directory isn't created unless you ask. That's what dash M is for, short for make home, and with it the folder finally appears. While you're there, dash S sets which shell they get. One short command, four separate changes. Forget dash M and that user logs straight into the root of the disk, owning nothing. Use useradd dash M dash S, or use adduser, which asks you the questions instead.

cmdUseradd.headline: useradd writes to [four places]
cmdUseradd.verdictSub: with no home directory of their own

scenes.narration: This user currently belongs to three groups, and you want to add a fourth. The command is user mod, and the flag combination is dash A capital G. The A stands for append, meaning add to what's already there, so docker is added and the other three stay exactly where they were. Now watch what happens if you forget that A. Capital G on its own doesn't mean add. User mod means replace the entire list with what follows, so sudo, W W W and dev are simply gone. And since sudo was one of them, that user is now locked out of administering the machine. And no warning is printed; the command reports success. One missing letter, and you've removed your own access. Read that flag out loud before you press return: dash A capital G, append.

stage.label: sudo is gone
stage.sub: and so are www and dev

scenes.narration: User del removes an account, and user del does exactly what you asked and nothing more. The account line disappears from etc passwd, so that person can no longer log in. But look at the disk. Their home directory is still sitting there, every file intact. And because the name that owned it no longer exists, the owner is now displayed as a bare number. The name is gone, but the numeric user I D it was attached to is still stamped on every one of those files. Add dash R and the home directory goes with the account. Which is why old servers are littered with folders owned by a number nobody recognises, and worse, a new account can be handed that same number later. If you're removing somebody properly, remove their files deliberately rather than leaving them behind.

cmdUserdel.headline: userdel leaves the [home directory]
cmdUserdel.verdictSub: which is why old servers are full of folders owned by 1004

scenes.narration: Everybody has typed this command at some point in their life, and almost nobody stops to think about where that password actually ends up. The command everyone knows is pass W D, and what it does next is the interesting part. What you type goes in one end. Pass W D passes through a one-way hash, maths that's easy forwards and effectively impossible backwards. The result is what gets written to the shadow file. What you typed is never stored anywhere. There's no route back along that arrow, by design. So when you log in later the system hashes your attempt and compares the two results, never the passwords themselves. So even a stolen shadow file gives up nobody's password, and that's the entire design. Nobody can give your password back, not even the administrator, which is why a reset is the only way in. So when somebody asks you to look up their password, the honest answer is that you can't.

cmdPasswd.headline: passwd stores a [hash], never the word

stage.label: there is no way back
stage.sub: the arrow only runs one way

cmdPasswd.verdict: Nobody can hand it back to you
cmdPasswd.verdictSub: not the admin, not the system — a reset is the only route

scenes.narration: Setting one password is fine. Setting a hundred of them by hand, on the morning a new team arrives and every account needs one, is not. Which is why ch pass W D exists. You give it a file of pairs, each line a username and the password it should get, fed down a pipe one line at a time. Ch pass W D works through them: deploy is set, C I is set, and ninety eight more follow in one pass. Now, you couldn't do this with pass W D, because pass W D deliberately insists on being run at a real terminal so that a password is never sitting in a script or a shell history. A password should never sit in a script or a history file, and that restriction is deliberate. Ch pass W D is the one built to be automated instead. Use passwd for a person at a keyboard, and chpasswd for a machine doing it in bulk.

cmdChpasswd.headline: chpasswd sets them [in bulk]

stage.label: never in a script
stage.sub: and never in your shell history

cmdChpasswd.verdictSub: which is deliberately the one thing passwd refuses to be

scenes.narration: Somebody else is on this server, and you'd like to know who they're and what they're up to, before you restart anything. The command which answers is W, which is the shortest on this whole list and covers both at once. Santhu is on P T S zero, in an editor. Deploy is on P T S one, running a sync. And here's dev again on P T S two, because they opened a second connection. That's two rows for one person, which trips people up constantly. These are sessions, not accounts. The header line across the top carries the load average, so you get a sense of the machine at the same time. W shows what each session is running and how long it has been idle. Who gives names and stops; W goes further. These are sessions, not accounts. Run w before you reboot anything, because somebody else may be halfway through something. Two rows for one person is normal, so read the TTY column before you assume anything.

cmdW.headline: w shows who is on [right now]

stage.label: w tells you more
stage.sub: which is usually what you wanted

cmdW.verdictSub: one person logged in twice is two rows, every time

scenes.narration: W tells you who's on the machine at this moment. The more useful question, once something has already gone wrong, is who was here earlier today, and last answers exactly that, going back weeks. Root signed in at twelve minutes past three in the morning, and whether or not that's fine, it's the row you stop on. Santhu logged in on Monday morning, which looks completely ordinary. The machine rebooted on Sunday evening. All of this comes from a log file called W T M P, which is worth knowing for one uncomfortable reason: a file can be edited by anyone who has root. So it's evidence rather than proof, and you check it early, before anything else gets touched. Last's the first place to look after a breach, and the first thing a competent attacker clears. Read last early, save the output somewhere else, and then start investigating.

cmdLast.headline: last reads the [login history]

stage.label: which means it can be edited

cmdLast.verdict: First place to look after a breach
cmdLast.verdictSub: and the first thing a competent attacker clears

scenes.narration: Sometimes you need a process to believe that one folder is the entire filesystem. The usual reason is repair: you've booted from a U S B stick and want to run commands as though you were inside the broken install. Ch root, short for change root, takes a directory and declares it the root for one process. From inside, everything above that directory simply stops existing. Run L S on slash and you see only the jail. Try to climb out with dot dot and you cannot, because there's nothing above you to climb into. But a root user inside can break out with the right system calls, because it was never built to contain a hostile process. Containers do that job properly, using kernel namespaces. Rescue work is what ch root is genuinely for. Treat it as isolation, never as security. Keep chroot for rescue work, and let containers do the job it was never built for. Reach for chroot when repairing a system, and a container when isolating one.

cmdChroot.headline: chroot is a fence, [not a wall]

steps.label: chroot /mnt/recovery /bin/bash
steps.detail: a new root for this shell

stage.label: so it is not a sandbox
stage.sub: it was never designed as one

stage.label: rescue work
stage.sub: is what it is genuinely for

cmdChroot.verdictSub: if you mean security, use a container

scenes.narration: Quick one. You change mod six four four a script, then run it. What happens? Have a think, and pause here if you need longer. Ready? It refuses. The execute bit is gone.

quiz.question: chmod 644 on a script, then run it?
quiz.why: 6 is read plus write. No execute bit, so it will not run.

scenes.narration: Drawer three is the lock. Change mod and change own set access. U mask shapes new files. Sudo lends power and logs it. The user tools manage the accounts behind it.

points.text: sudo lends power, and logs it

scenes.narration: Drawer four. What's running, and how you stop it without losing work.

P S is short for process status, and P S hands you a snapshot of everything running at this exact instant. Not a live view, a still photograph. Each row is a process, so here's P I D four eight two one, which is node running your application, P I D one one four zero, which is engine X, and right at the top P I D one, systemd, the ancestor of every other process on the box. Of everything in that output, the P I D column is the one to find. P S dash E F prints the same data in a different syntax, because two flavours of Unix disagreed about flags forty years ago and both won. Every other tool on this list will ask you for that number. Get comfortable finding a PID quickly, because almost everything after this needs one.

cmdPs.headline: ps is a [snapshot], not a feed
cmdPs.verdict: Every other tool wants the PID
cmdPs.verdictSub: which is why you learn to spot it fast

scenes.narration: P S gives you a flat list, which hides the most useful fact about processes: every one of them was started by another one. P S tree draws that instead. At the top sits systemd, process number one, which the kernel started before anything else. Engine X was started by systemd. A worker was started by engine X. Those connecting lines are real relationships, not decoration. Now kill a parent in the middle and the line to it snaps, but its children aren't killed along with it. Instead process one adopts them, immediately and automatically. Nothing is ever left without a parent, which is exactly how a job can outlive the shell that launched it. Whenever a process seems to have no parent, pstree shows you it was adopted rather than orphaned.

cmdPstree.headline: pstree shows [who started whom]

stage.label: the children survive
stage.sub: they are not killed with it

cmdPstree.verdict: Nothing is ever left without a parent
cmdPstree.verdictSub: which is how a process can outlive the shell that started it

scenes.narration: P S shows you an instant. The question you usually have is what's happening now, and which needs something that moves, which is top. Top shows the same processes, but it refreshes every couple of seconds instead of printing once. So node is climbing hard, postgres is steady and clearly not your problem, and engine X is almost idle. And crucially the rows re-sort as it goes, so whatever is busiest keeps rising to the top on its own. You don't read this output so much as watch it. Press Q to leave. Top's the first thing to open on a slow box, because top shows you the shape of a problem rather than a single number. Watch top for ten seconds before you conclude anything, because one frame tells you very little.

cmdTop.headline: top re-sorts [as you watch]

steps.label: top
steps.detail: press q to leave, M to sort by memory

cmdTop.verdict: The first thing you open on a slow box
cmdTop.verdictSub: because it shows you the shape of a problem, not one number

scenes.narration: Top works, but it makes you do arithmetic in your head, it'll not let you touch the mouse, and killing something means typing a number by hand. H top is that tool with the edges filed off. Across the top you get one bar per processor core, so a load of four on eight cores looks like what it is. The colours in those bars separate kernel work from your own. Below, the process list is the same, except you can click a row with the mouse and press F nine to kill it, no P I D required. And you can scroll sideways for the full command line, or press F five for the tree view. Same numbers, far less squinting, and worth installing on every machine you look after. Install htop on any machine you'll spend real time on. You'll stop opening top entirely.

cmdHtop.headline: htop is top with [colour and a mouse]

stage.label: one bar per core
stage.sub: so you see which cores are loaded

cmdHtop.verdictSub: worth installing on every machine you administer

scenes.narration: Top and H top both show this instant, refreshed every couple of seconds. Useful, but a number which keeps changing still only ever describes right now. B top plots that same information over time, which changes what you can see. Processor use is drawn across the last minute, memory climbs steadily, and the network is flat. Compare that to what top would tell you. A number describes this second and nothing more. A line tells you where it's heading, which is nearly always what you needed. That steady climb isn't a value to worry about yet; it's a leak, and it'll matter within the hour. Disk throughput is plotted on that same timeline. A spike you can see coming beats a reading which only describes this second. Use btop when the question is where this is heading rather than where it is.

cmdBtop.headline: btop draws it [over time]

stage.label: a line tells you the direction

cmdBtop.verdict: A spike you can see coming
cmdBtop.verdictSub: an instant reading always hides the trend

scenes.narration: Here's the situation every one of these live tools fails at. The server was slow at twenty to three this afternoon. A top is fine now. What happened? A top solves it, because it has been quietly writing all these numbers to disk the whole time. Replay yesterday and two o'clock looks entirely normal. Move forward and twenty to three is your spike, and critically it recorded which processes were running at that moment as well. By ten past three it had recovered on its own. Top can't answer any of that, because top only ever knows about now. These are the only questions you get after an outage, which makes a top the one worth enabling in advance. Install atop today, and the next outage will be one you can actually investigate.

cmdAtop.headline: atop already [recorded it]
cmdAtop.verdict: It answers questions after the fact
cmdAtop.verdictSub: which is the only kind you get after an outage

scenes.narration: Every tool so far assumes you already know what to look at. That's a fair assumption after ten years and a terrible one on your first week. Glances puts every subsystem on a single screen and colours whichever is in trouble. Processor is fine. Memory is fine. Disk input and output is saturated, and it has gone red. Network is fine. You didn't have to know that the disk was the suspect, because glances applies the threshold for you, and the red panel finds you rather than the other way round. When you're new, not knowing which tool to open is the actual problem, and this is the honest answer to it. Glances is the one to reach for when you know something is wrong but not what.

cmdGlances.headline: glances shows [everything] at once

stage.label: it picks the threshold
stage.sub: so you do not have to

cmdGlances.verdict: You do not need to know which tool to open
cmdGlances.verdictSub: which is exactly the problem when you are new

scenes.narration: Every tool up to this point decided its own layout, and you either liked it or you did not. That's fine until the layout hides the one panel you need. N mon works the other way round entirely: it starts almost empty and you assemble the view you want by pressing keys. Press C and a processor panel docks into place. Press M and memory joins it. D for disk, N for network. You build exactly the dashboard this problem needs, wasting nothing on panels you're not reading. But the reason it has survived since the nineteen nineties is the other mode. Dash F writes all of it to a file instead of drawing anything at all, so you can leave it overnight and graph it later in a spreadsheet. N mon was built for capture rather than watching, which is still unusual. Leave nmon recording overnight and you'll have a graph instead of a guess in the morning.

cmdNmon.headline: nmon builds the view [you want]

steps.label: nmon
steps.detail: then press c, m, d, n

stage.label: press c
stage.sub: and a CPU panel docks in

stage.label: graph it later
stage.sub: in a spreadsheet, if you like

cmdNmon.verdict: Built for capture, not just for watching
cmdNmon.verdictSub: which is why it survived from 1997

scenes.narration: The name is misleading, so start here: kill doesn't destroy anything. Kill sends a signal, and a signal is a message. Run it plainly and it sends sig term, which politely asks a process to stop. The process receives that message and gets to decide what to do about it, so typically it flushes what it was writing, closes its files and exits on its own terms. Now dash nine is different. That's sig kill, and sig kill can't be caught or ignored, because the kernel removes the process without ever delivering the message. Kill never gets the chance to save, so whatever was in memory is gone. Send sig term first, every single time. If sig term hasn't worked after ten seconds, the process is stuck, and only then use dash nine.

cmdKill.headline: kill sends a [signal], not a bullet

stage.label: the process catches it
stage.sub: and it can choose to act

cmdKill.verdictSub: -9 is what you try when nothing else worked

scenes.narration: Kill needs a process I D, and when eight copies of the same program are running, hunting down all eight of those numbers by hand gets old fast. Kill all works by name instead, and that's the whole difference. So node running as four eight two one goes, node as four eight two two goes, and so does node as five three one zero, which a colleague started and is two hours into. All three matched the name, so all three were signalled, and it never asked you which ones you actually meant. On your own laptop this is a convenience. On a shared server it's genuinely dangerous, so P kill with a user filter is the habit worth building instead. Match on a name, and you match everybody's. On anything shared, find the PIDs and kill those. Naming them takes ten more seconds and costs nobody an afternoon.

cmdKillall.headline: killall hits [all of them]
cmdKillall.verdictSub: genuinely dangerous on a shared server

scenes.narration: You start a long backup, close the laptop, come back, and the job died. Here's why. Run something in the background normally, and when you close the terminal or the connection drops, a signal called hangup is sent to every job that terminal started. Your plain background job receives it and stops. The fix is in the name: no hup is short for no hangup, and a job started under it simply ignores that signal, so it carries on running with the terminal long gone. One thing to expect: since there's no screen to print to any more, its output is written into a file called nohup dot out. That file is where people forget to look. Better still, use screen or tmux, which we'll get to, and you keep the output as well.

cmdNohup.headline: nohup ignores the [hangup]

stage.label: output goes to nohup.out
stage.sub: since there is no screen left

cmdNohup.verdictSub: but check nohup.out, because that is where the output went

scenes.narration: Sleep pauses for a fixed time, and it's the least interesting command here until you look at how it does it. Your script runs down its lines, reaches the sleep and stops. Five seconds pass with nothing happening at all, and here's the part worth noticing: the processor sits at zero throughout, because sleep asks the kernel to wake it later and then genuinely stops running. Sleep is not counting in a loop. Then the next line runs, exactly where it left off. And you're not limited to seconds, since it takes minutes, hours and days as well. Because it truly blocks, a sleep inside a retry loop costs you nothing. Sleep is what makes a retry loop polite instead of a machine hammering a server.

cmdSleep.headline: sleep pauses [the script]

steps.label: sleep 2m
steps.detail: m, h and d also work

cmdSleep.verdictSub: which is why a sleep in a loop is not wasteful

scenes.narration: Two jobs, and you want them running at the same time. Start job A, which takes three seconds, and job B, which takes seven, and put an ampersand after each to send them into the background. Now here's the bug, and it's subtle because nothing looks broken. The script carries straight on, reaches its end and exits, while job B still has four seconds of work left. Your C I run goes green on work which never finished. The fix is one word: wait holds the script until every background child has completed, so its exit status finally means something. Without it, your script reports success on work that's still running. One word at the end of a script is the difference between a real result and a lie.

cmdWait.headline: wait holds until [they finish]

steps.label: wait
steps.detail: hold here until both are done

cmdWait.verdict: Without it, your script reports success early
cmdWait.verdictSub: on work that had not finished yet

scenes.narration: You try to unmount a disk and it refuses with target is busy, which tells you nothing useful. L S O F, short for list open files, tells you who's responsible. Tail is holding a log file open on that disk. Vim is holding a config. Those two handles are the entire reason the unmount failed. Now the clever part. On Linux a network socket is a kind of file as well, genuinely, not by analogy. So the same tool with dash I shows you engine X holding port four four three, which means one command answers both questions. The next time something says address already in use, this is the fastest way to find out what. Lsof is the tool which turns a useless error message into a process you can name.

cmdLsof.headline: lsof names the [holder]

stage.label: tail, PID 4821
stage.sub: is holding a log file open

stage.label: a socket is a file too

cmdLsof.verdictSub: lsof -i is the fastest answer to that error

scenes.narration: A program fails with an error which makes no sense. S trace shows you what it's actually doing, because every real thing a program does goes through the kernel. Opening a file, reading a socket, all of it. So open this file is a request you can watch, and the kernel answers no such file or directory. Meanwhile the program prints something about a database connection, which is why you were confused. The catch is that thousands of these scroll past. So add dash E to filter down to just the calls you care about, and there it is, a config path that doesn't exist. S trace failed on a missing file, not on the thing it told you. Strace is a big hammer, so reach for it when the error message has already lied to you.

cmdStrace.headline: strace shows what it [really tried]

stage.label: -e filters them
stage.sub: to just the ones you care about

stage.label: there it is
stage.sub: a config path that does not exist

cmdStrace.verdict: It failed on a missing file
cmdStrace.verdictSub: not on whatever its error message claimed

scenes.narration: Quick one. A process is ignoring your kill entirely. Which signal can't be ignored? Have a think, and pause here if you need longer. Ready? Sig kill, because the kernel delivers it.

quiz.question: Which signal can a process NOT ignore?
quiz.why: The kernel delivers SIGKILL. The program never gets a say.

scenes.narration: Drawer four is control. P S and P S tree list them. Top shows them moving. Kill signals them politely. L S O F and S trace find the cause, so nothing stays mysterious.

points.text: top and htop show it live
lsof and strace find the cause

scenes.narration: Drawer five. Watching the machine properly, so you're not guessing.

Load average is the most consistently misread number in all of Linux, and it appears in almost every tool here, so let's fix it properly now. Up time gives you three numbers rather than one, and the three are the point. The first is the last minute, the second is the last five minutes, and the third is the last fifteen. Read them together as a direction of travel. Now the part people get wrong. A load of four sounds alarming until you ask how many cores this machine has. On eight cores that's half busy: four slots working, four sitting free. On two cores, the very same figure means badly overloaded, with work queuing up behind. Always divide by your core count, because the number on its own tells you nothing. Load is a queue length, not a percentage, and that one sentence fixes most of the confusion.

cmdUptime.headline: Load is [three numbers], not one
cmdUptime.verdict: Always divide by your core count
cmdUptime.verdictSub: the number alone means nothing at all

scenes.narration: The first time you run this particular command on a perfectly healthy server, you'll be completely convinced the machine is about to fall over. Free reports two hundred megabytes free on a server with thirty two gigabytes. That looks alarming, and it's completely fine. Here's why. Used is your programs, genuinely occupied. Cache is memory Linux borrowed to keep recently read files close by, and it'll hand every byte of it back the moment something needs it. Free is memory doing nothing whatsoever, which is memory being wasted. And available is the figure you actually wanted: what a new program could have right now. Ask for memory and the cache simply shrinks. Read available and ignore free. Free memory on a Linux box is wasted memory, and the kernel is doing you a favour.

cmdFree.headline: Low free memory is [normal]

stage.label: cache
stage.sub: borrowed, and handed back on demand

cmdFree.verdictSub: Linux spends idle memory on purpose, because idle memory helps nobody

scenes.narration: You want to know whether this machine is genuinely short of memory, and you want to watch it change rather than take a single reading. That tool is V M stat. There's one trap to know about first. The very first row is an average since the machine booted, so ignore it completely; it's history, not a reading. The second row is the first real one, and one follows every second. The columns to watch are S I and S O, swap in and swap out, which count memory being pushed to disk and pulled back. Zero there's healthy. Anything above zero means the machine is genuinely short of memory. That's pressure, not just usage, and it's the difference between slow and about to fall over. Watch the swap columns for ten seconds, and you'll know whether memory is the real problem.

cmdVmstat.headline: vmstat's first row is [since boot]

stage.label: ignore it
stage.sub: it is not a reading of now

cmdVmstat.verdict: Non-zero swap is the red flag
cmdVmstat.verdictSub: it means shortage, not merely usage

scenes.narration: The processor is sitting almost idle and yet the whole machine feels like it's wading through treacle. Nine times out of ten that's the disk, and I O stat is how you confirm it. I O stat reports per device, so you get reads in megabytes a second and writes, which are heavy here but expected for a database. On throughput alone this disk looks perfectly healthy, and that's exactly the trap. The column which matters is await, which measures how long each request sat waiting before the disk even started on it. A long queue is what slowness actually feels like from inside a program. So when await climbs while throughput stays modest, the disk is your bottleneck. Low throughput with high await means saturated, not idle. When the CPU looks idle and everything feels slow, await is the number to go and read.

cmdIostat.headline: await is the number [that matters]

stage.label: time spent queuing
stage.sub: before the request is even served

stage.label: a long queue
stage.sub: is what slow actually feels like

cmdIostat.verdictSub: means the disk is saturated even though the numbers look small

scenes.narration: I O stat told you the disk is saturated, which is useful and immediately raises the obvious next question: saturated by what, exactly? I O top answers that, because knowing a disk is busy without knowing who made it busy leaves you nowhere. Here postgres is writing eighty eight megabytes a second, which is your answer. R sync is doing twelve, which is the backup you scheduled and expected. Everything else is doing essentially nothing. The dash O flag shows only processes actually doing input and output, rather than filling the screen with idle ones. Now you've a process I D and a decision. Every monitoring tool tells you something is wrong; this one tells you who. Iostat and iotop are a pair: one finds the problem, the other names who caused it.

cmdIotop.headline: iotop names the [writer]

stage.label: iostat said busy
stage.sub: but not who made it busy

cmdIotop.verdict: iostat says busy, iotop says who
cmdIotop.verdictSub: which is always the next question you were going to ask

scenes.narration: The problem with running four monitoring tools in four separate windows is that none of them agree on when now actually is. D stat fixes that by putting several subsystems on one line: processor split into user and system time, disk reads and writes, and network sent and received. Crucially they're all sampled at the same instant, on the same tick. Which means when you see a disk spike in this column, and a processor wait sitting in the very same column, you're looking at genuine correlation rather than two readings you're trying to line up by eye. One time axis for everything is how you stop guessing at cause and effect. Dstat is what you leave running while you reproduce something, because the columns line up.

cmdDstat.headline: dstat puts it [on one line]
cmdDstat.verdictSub: which is how you stop guessing at cause and effect

scenes.narration: S A R is the tool that absolutely everybody forgets about, and it's also the one which will save you on the day it genuinely counts. S A R, which is the system activity reporter, writes these numbers to disk every ten minutes of every day whether anyone is watching or not. So after an outage you can pick a day, even one from weeks ago, and simply read what happened. Two o'clock was normal. Twenty to three is your spike. By ten past three it had recovered. But here's the catch which catches everyone. Look at the days before you switched it on and they're empty, because you can't record the past retrospectively. Enable sysstat before you need it, because the outage always arrives before the monitoring does. Turn sysstat on across your machines this week, and thank yourself during the next incident.

cmdSar.headline: sar already [wrote it down]

stage.label: pick a day
stage.sub: from weeks ago if you like

cmdSar.verdict: Enable sysstat before you need it
cmdSar.verdictSub: the outage always comes before the monitoring does

scenes.narration: Sometimes the tool you need doesn't exist, and watch is how you build it in about four seconds. Watch takes any command at all and runs it exactly as you typed it, shows you the output, then waits and runs it again. That's the whole idea. And it matters because a single reading of anything tells you almost nothing. Add dash D and it'll highlight whatever changed since the previous run, so when a number creeps upward run after run, the leak becomes obvious without you installing anything. Watch turns any command into a live dashboard, which is why you rarely need a purpose-built tool for a one-off question. Any time you find yourself pressing up and return repeatedly, watch is the command you wanted.

cmdWatch.headline: watch turns anything [into a dashboard]

stage.label: now the leak is obvious
stage.sub: and it took no tooling at all

cmdWatch.verdict: It turns any command into a dashboard
cmdWatch.verdictSub: which means you never need a purpose-built tool for a one-off

scenes.narration: Quick one. Load reads four, on eight cores. Problem, or fine? Have a think, and pause here if you need longer. Ready? Fine, because load counts against cores.

quiz.question: Load 4.0 on an 8-core box?
quiz.why: Load is measured against core count. Four of eight is about half.

scenes.narration: Drawer five is your eyes on the machine. Up time and free give the headline. V M stat and I O stat give the detail. S A R remembers yesterday. Watch makes anything live, so you're never guessing.
Drawer six. Disks, filesystems, and the one command that deserves fear.

D F is short for disk free, and dash H shows you how full each filesystem is. Sixty two percent, so there's plenty of room, which makes it very strange which writes are failing. Here's what's happening. Every single file on the disk needs an inode, a small record holding its permissions, owner and location. The number of inodes is fixed when the filesystem is created and it never grows. So run D F dash I and inodes are at a hundred percent. Millions of tiny files, a session cache perhaps, consumed one inode each. The disk is full of names rather than of data. You've free space and nowhere to put anything. So when writes fail on a disk with space left, df dash I is the second thing you run.

cmdDf.headline: df -i is the [trap] nobody checks

stage.label: inodes are a fixed number
stage.sub: set when the filesystem was made

stage.label: the disk is full of names

cmdDf.verdict: Space free, and still out of room
cmdDf.verdictSub: df -h is the habit; df -i is the one that finds this

scenes.narration: D F told you the disk is full. D U, short for disk usage, tells you what filled it, because D U measures by directory rather than by filesystem. So at the top level var log is by far the biggest, home is twenty six gigabytes, user is eighteen. That's the difference between the two commands in one line. Now, don't guess from here. Run it again one level deeper, pointed at var log itself, and var log engine X is the actual culprit, holding forty one gigabytes of access logs nobody rotated. Walk down one level at a time and the answer falls out. D F says it's full; D U says what filled it. Df then du then ncdu is the sequence, and it narrows the answer every step.

cmdDu.headline: du finds [which directory] ate it
cmdDu.verdict: df tells you it is full
cmdDu.verdictSub: du tells you what filled it

scenes.narration: D U works, but in practice you end up typing the same command three times over, with a longer path on each attempt. Now run it without dash L and you're in the editor proper, and this is the part which makes it approachable. Every change you make happens to a copy held in memory, not to the disk. Add partitions, delete them, change types. Nothing is real until you press W to write. And if you've made a mess, press Q and absolutely nothing happened. Which is why F disk is safer to explore than its reputation suggests. Because nothing is written until W, fdisk dash L is safe to run anywhere, any time.

scenes.narration: You plug in a four terabyte disk and F disk gets awkward about it. Here's why. M B R, the old partition table format, uses thirty two bits to address blocks on the disk. That sounds like a lot, and with five hundred and twelve byte blocks it runs out at two terabytes. Not a policy, not a bug; the field is simply not wide enough to describe a larger disk. G P T is the replacement, and it uses sixty four bits instead, which is a difference so large it stops being worth discussing. So your four terabyte disk needs G P T, and parted is the tool which writes one, since F disk was built for the older format. Over two terabytes, M B R physically cannot. Use parted for anything modern, and treat MBR as something you only meet on old disks.

scenes.narration: Here's a failure that ruins somebody's morning roughly once a year, and it's entirely avoidable once you know that this one small command exists. Blk I D prints every block device with its filesystem type and its U U I D. Today this partition is slash dev slash S D B one. The trouble is that a name like that describes a position, not an identity. Plug a U S B stick in and reboot, and the names shuffle: what was S D B is now S D C. Anything in fstab pointing at the old name now points at the wrong disk. But the U U I D never changes, because it's written into the filesystem itself. So put U U I Ds in fstab, never device names. Anything you want mounted at boot goes in fstab by UUID, and it will still be there next year.

scenes.narration: A partition is just a region of a disk; on its own it can't hold files at all. Something has to write the structure which turns it into a filesystem, and that something is make F S. Before you run it the partition holds your data. As it runs it writes structure: inode tables, superblocks, the bookkeeping a filesystem needs to exist. Note what it doesn't do. Make F S doesn't erase your files. Make F S simply stops referring to them, which is why the old blocks become unreachable rather than destroyed, and why recovery tools sometimes work. What you're left with is an empty filesystem, ready to mount. And like most of this drawer, there's no confirmation prompt whatsoever. So read the device name twice before you press return. scenes.narration: F S C K, short for filesystem check, looks for damage and repairs it. Run it on a live disk and it warns you that the device is mounted. That warning isn't boilerplate, and people ignore it constantly. The reason it matters is this: the kernel is still writing to that filesystem while F S C K is reading it, so F S C K makes decisions from a picture that's already out of date, and repairs things which were never broken. That corrupts the disk you were trying to fix. So unmount it first, always. Then it sweeps the inode table and the block map properly, and an orphaned inode gets reattached into lost plus found. Never run it on something mounted. Unmount, then check, then mount again. In that order, fsck is a repair rather than a risk.

You pick a folder, here M N T data, which is just an ordinary directory. The new disk is grafted onto that point, and its contents now appear there as though they always had. Now the part that confuses people. If that folder already had files in it, they're hidden underneath the mount. Hidden, not deleted, and completely untouched. Unmount the disk and they reappear exactly as they were. One tree, not one per disk, which is why Linux has no drive letters to remember. Mount an empty directory, always, and you'll never wonder where your files went.

So L S O F names the culprit: tail is holding a log file open on that disk, and until that process lets go, nothing else is going to happen here. Kill it and the handle closes, so the unmount works first time. What you shouldn't do is reach straight for dash F to force it, because there may be writes sitting in memory that haven't reached the disk yet, and forcing throws them away. If you genuinely can't stop the process, dash L is the gentler option; it detaches the filesystem and finishes the job once the last handle closes. The refusal is protecting data. When a disk won't unmount, lsof answers it in one command, so reach for that instead of force. Lsof first, kill second, unmount third. That order never loses a write.

scenes.narration: When something won't connect, this is the first thing anyone reaches for, and most people only ever read half of what it tells them. The command is ping, and what it does is simple: a packet leaves your machine, crosses the gateway, and the far end replies, here in twelve milliseconds. Do it four times and you learn two separate things. The first is how far away it is. The second is more important. Watch packet three: it leaves and never comes back. That's loss, which is a completely different problem from slowness. One packet in four missing will make a connection feel broken even though the average time still looks perfectly healthy. So read the loss figure first, because the average hides it. Run ping with dash C four, read the loss line first, and the latency second.

scenes.narration: Ping tells you whether the far end is reachable, but when it's not, it says nothing about where along the way things went wrong. Trace route tells you the whole path, and the trick behind it's genuinely clever. Trace route sends a packet allowed to travel exactly one hop, which expires immediately and the router that killed it politely reports back. That gives you hop one, your own router. Then it allows two hops, then three, walking outward one at a time. So hop four is your internet provider, hop seven answers with nothing whatsoever, and hop nine is the destination. Now, about hop seven. Those stars aren't automatically a fault, because plenty of routers are configured never to reply, and your traffic passes straight through them regardless. Traceroute tells you where the path goes; it takes judgement to say where it breaks.

scenes.narration: Trace route has a real weakness: it runs once and then stops. If your problem is intermittent, a single pass will very often miss it entirely. M T R is trace route and ping combined, so it keeps probing every hop, hundreds of times, and builds up statistics. Now the picture is much clearer. Hop four is dropping nothing. Hop seven is dropping thirty eight percent of packets. But look at hop nine, which is clean again, and that's the actual clue. If loss at one hop clears at the next, that router is almost certainly just rate limiting its own replies rather than dropping your traffic. One run can lie. A hundred runs cannot. Leave mtr running for a minute before you phone anybody about a network problem.

The problem is how it gets it: net stat reads through the proc filesystem, one file per connection, and on a server with thousands of connections that's thousands of reads. That's what you check first when a service won't answer. Now filter by state instead and the listeners drop away, leaving an established connection, which is a conversation actually in progress with a real peer at the other end. Here's the diagnostic that saves you an afternoon. If S S says a service is listening and yet nothing can reach it, the problem isn't the application; it's a firewall, a security group, or the address it bound to. Wired backup is a second profile for that very same device. So a device is hardware and it doesn't change, while a profile is configuration and you can keep as many as you like. When you bring a profile up, it snaps onto the device, and switching between them changes the machine's entire network identity without you touching a cable. One device, many profiles. D N S turns a name into an address, and when it goes wrong you need to see the whole exchange. Dig is short for domain information groper. You ask a resolver, here one dot one dot one dot one, and it answers. What comes back is an A record, which maps the name to an address. Alongside it sits a T T L of three hundred, meaning cache this answer for five minutes, which is exactly why a D N S change doesn't appear everywhere at once. If you only want the value, plus short strips all of it away. But the full output is the point: it tells you who answered and how long that answer stays true. cmdCurl.verdictSub: no client library, no framework, no guessing in between
