scenes.narration: Drawer nine. Archives, scheduled jobs, and sessions that survive because you won't.

Tar is the most googled command on this entire list, and honestly that's avoidable. The name is short for tape archive, from back when which was literal. Those four letters after the dash are four separate instructions wearing one coat, so let's take them apart. C creates a new archive, gathering many files into one. Z compresses that archive using gzip. V is verbose, printing each name as it goes in. And F names the output file, which is why F always comes last: whatever follows it's the filename. Now the part that saves you. Swap the C for an X and the whole thing runs backwards and extracts, while the other three letters stay exactly as they were. X to extract, C to create. Tar dash X Z V F to extract, tar dash C Z V F to create, and you're done with tar.

cmdTar.headline: czvf is [four instructions]

stage.label: f logs.tar.gz
stage.sub: the output file, and f must come last

cmdTar.verdictSub: which is genuinely the whole of what you need to remember

scenes.narration: Gzip, which is short for G N U zip, shrinks a single file, and it's very good at it: forty one megabytes of log goes in and six megabytes comes out. But there's a behaviour here which catches everybody exactly once. The original file is gone. Gzip didn't make a copy alongside it; it replaced it, and you now have only the compressed version. That surprises people every single time, particularly inside a script that expected to read the original afterwards. So add dash K, for keep, and both files survive. And it's quick: that took about a second. Gzip replaces by default, so learn dash K before you need it rather than after. Use dash K whenever a script downstream still expects the original file to be there.

cmdGzip.headline: gzip [replaces] the original
cmdGzip.verdict: It replaces the file by default
cmdGzip.verdictSub: so -k is the flag to remember before you need it

scenes.narration: Gzip is fast, and for almost anything you compress it's good enough. Every so often you want the file as small as it'll go. That's when you reach for B zip two. Run both against the same log. Gzip finishes in a second, giving six megabytes. B zip two takes eight and a half, giving four and a half. You're paying seven times the processor time for a megabyte and a half. Whether that's worth it depends on what happens next. For a log you rotate nightly, it's a waste. For an archive you keep for seven years, it's obviously right. Write once, read almost never, is where it pays. X Z goes further still. But gzip stays the default, because it's fast enough and always installed. Match the compressor to how often you pay the cost back. Gzip for anything you touch often, bzip2 or xz for anything you're storing and forgetting.

cmdBzip2.headline: bzip2 trades [time] for size

stage.label: seven times slower
stage.sub: for a megabyte and a half

stage.label: an archive you keep for years

cmdBzip2.verdict: Worth it for archives, not for logs
cmdBzip2.verdictSub: the question is how often you will pay the cost back

scenes.narration: You've an archive which needs to go to somebody who has quite honestly never opened a terminal window in their entire life. Zip is what they can open, and the difference from tar dot gz is structural. A tar dot gz is a single compressed stream, so to reach one file in the middle you've to decompress everything before it. Zip compresses each file separately and keeps an index at the end of the archive. That means you can pull one file straight out without touching the rest. And it opens with a double click on any operating system. So the rule is really about who opens it. Send zip to people and tar dot gz to servers.

cmdZip.headline: zip is the [portable] one

stage.label: and keeps an index
stage.sub: at the end of the archive

stage.label: and it opens by double click

cmdZip.verdict: Send zip to people, tar.gz to servers
cmdZip.verdictSub: the format you choose is really about who opens it

scenes.narration: Scheduling on Linux comes down to one line of five numbers, and almost everybody copies that line from somewhere else without ever reading it properly. Cron is five fields in a fixed order, and that order is the whole trick. The first field is the minute, zero to fifty nine. The second is the hour, zero to twenty three. The third is the day of the month. The fourth is the month. The fifth is the day of the week, where zero is Sunday. Then a star simply means every one of whatever that field counts. So this line means half past two in the morning, on Mondays only. Five stars means every single minute of every day, which is how people take servers down by accident. Read the five fields left to right, and any cron line becomes plain English.

cmdCron.headline: cron is [five fields]

stage.label: field 5
stage.sub: day of the week, 0 is Sunday

cmdCron.verdict: Five stars is every single minute
cmdCron.verdictSub: which is the classic way to accidentally take a server down

scenes.narration: Cron is the schedule; crontab is how you edit it. Dash E opens your table in an editor, and the important bit is that it validates the file when you save. A syntax error is rejected there and then, with a message telling you. Now compare that with editing the crontab file directly on disk, which people do all the time. That skips the check completely, and cron will simply skip the broken job, silently, forever. No email, no log entry, nothing. Which is why dash L matters: it prints what's actually loaded right now, and that's the only real proof your job exists. A schedule you never verified isn't a schedule. Always use crontab dash E, then crontab dash L to confirm what actually got installed.

cmdCrontab.headline: crontab -e, never [edit the file]

steps.label: crontab -e
steps.detail: opens your table in an editor

stage.label: crontab -e
stage.sub: opens your table in an editor

stage.label: a bad line is rejected
stage.sub: and you are told about it

cmdCrontab.verdictSub: nothing emails you, nothing logs it, the job simply never runs

scenes.narration: A script is just a file with commands in it, and yet the first time you run one you get permission denied. Here's why. New files aren't created executable, because which would be a terrible default. So change mod plus X flips exactly that one bit, and the very same command now works. Two more details. The first line of the script names the interpreter that should run it, and that line is called the shebang. And you have to write dot slash in front of the name, because the current folder is deliberately not in your search path. That's a security decision: if it were, dropping a file called L S into a shared directory would hijack everyone's commands. Shebang, chmod plus X, then dot slash. Three things, and your script runs anywhere.

cmdBashscript.headline: Three lines and a [permission bit]

stage.label: permission denied
stage.sub: on a file you just wrote

stage.label: the execute bit
stage.sub: is not set on new files

stage.label: ./ is required
stage.sub: because . is not in your PATH

cmdBashscript.verdict: The current folder is deliberately not in PATH
cmdBashscript.verdictSub: so a file named ls in a shared folder cannot hijack your commands

scenes.narration: Alias binds a long command to a short name, and the trap is about where that binding lives. Type it at the prompt and it works straight away, but only inside this one shell, and only until you close it. Open a new terminal and it has gone. If you want it to outlive the session, append it to your bashrc, which every new shell reads on startup, and now it survives forever. But here's the one which catches people. A script still can't see your aliases, because a script runs a non-interactive shell and bashrc isn't read at all. Which is exactly why a command that works perfectly when you type it fails the moment cron runs the same line. Put your aliases in bashrc, and put the real command in your scripts.

cmdAlias.headline: An alias dies unless you [save it]

stage.label: but only in this shell
stage.sub: and only until you close it

cmdAlias.verdict: Your scripts do not inherit your aliases
cmdAlias.verdictSub: which is exactly why a command works for you and fails in cron

scenes.narration: Env shows the variables a command inherits when it starts. Path tells the shell where to look for commands. Home is your home directory. And every process you start inherits a copy of this whole set, which is how configuration reaches a program without a config file. Now the genuinely useful trick here. Put debug equals one in front of a command and you've set that variable for that process alone, and for anything it starts. The very next command you type has no debug at all. Nothing else on the machine ever saw it. That matters on a shared box, because exporting a secret into your shell leaves it sitting in the environment of everything you run afterwards. Setting a variable in front of a command is the safest way to try something once.

cmdEnv.headline: env changes it for [one command]
cmdEnv.verdict: It never leaks past that one command
cmdEnv.verdictSub: which is why it is safe to use on a machine other people share

scenes.narration: History keeps everything you've typed, numbered, and there are three ways to reach back into it. Bang followed by a number runs that exact line again. Bang bang runs the previous command. And the one you'll genuinely use every day is this: you run something, it fails because it needed privilege, and rather than retype any of it you just run sudo bang bang. Better still, control R searches backwards through your history as you type. One warning, though. All of this is written to a file in your home directory, so any password you ever typed as part of a command is sitting on disk in plain text. Which is a good reason never to put one on a command line. Sudo bang bang will save you more typing this year than any other two words here.

cmdHistory.headline: history plus [Ctrl-R]

stage.label: sudo !!
stage.sub: the one you will actually use

stage.label: it is written to a file

cmdHistory.verdict: sudo !! is the one worth learning
cmdHistory.verdictSub: run that again, but with privilege, without retyping a word

scenes.narration: Start a long job over S S H and it dies when the connection drops, because your session belongs to that connection and when it closes, everything inside goes with it. Screen fixes that properly. Dash capital S creates a session which lives on the server itself, and the job runs inside that session rather than inside your connection. So now your connection can drop, your laptop can sleep, and the work carries straight on. When you come back, screen dash R reattaches you and everything is exactly where you left it. And control A then D detaches deliberately. The session belongs to the server, not to you, which is the whole point. Start anything long inside screen or tmux, and a dropped connection stops mattering.

cmdScreen.headline: screen survives your [dropped wifi]

stage.label: screen -S
stage.sub: creates a session on the server

cmdScreen.verdict: The session belongs to the server
cmdScreen.verdictSub: which is why the job survives your laptop going to sleep

scenes.narration: T mux does everything screen does, so you get the same survival across a dropped connection, and then T mux splits the terminal into panes. That sounds cosmetic until you use it. One pane holds your editor. Another holds the logs, live, as you work. T mux's one session holding both, so you're watching your change and its effect at the same time without switching windows. Attach by name from any machine and the whole layout comes back. One practical note: control B is the prefix key for everything in T mux, where screen uses control A. The muscle memory doesn't transfer between them, so pick one and commit to it. Tmux is worth an afternoon of practice, because it changes how you work on servers.

cmdTmux.headline: tmux adds [panes] to the same idea
cmdTmux.verdict: Learn one of the two, properly
cmdTmux.verdictSub: the muscle memory does not transfer, so pick and commit

scenes.narration: Here's the distinction which catches people out, and getting the two confused costs them an outage. A service has two separate switches, not one. Here it's stopped. Start it and it's running right now, serving traffic, completely fine. But it'll not come back after a reboot, because that's the other switch. Enable is the one that makes it start at boot, and it doesn't start it now. So reboot this machine and only the service you enabled comes back on its own. Status shows you both states at once, which is why it's the command to run when something isn't behaving. You almost always want both, and enable dash dash now does the pair in one go. Systemctl enable dash dash now is the command you actually wanted, nearly every time.

cmdSystemctl.headline: start is now. [enable] is after reboot
cmdSystemctl.verdictSub: which is almost always what you actually meant

scenes.narration: The mistake with journal C T L is treating it like a file and scrolling. Journal C T L's a database, and you query it. Dash U narrows to one service, which is usually the first thing you want. Add dash B and you only see this boot, so yesterday's noise disappears. Add dash P err and you only see errors and worse. Three filters, and what's left is the thing you were looking for. And when you want to watch it happen, dash F follows the journal live, exactly like tail dash F on a log file. The habit worth building is composing filters rather than scrolling, because every flag narrows the set and they stack. Compose the filters and journalctl goes from overwhelming to the fastest log tool you own.

cmdJournalctl.headline: journalctl is [filters], not scrolling

Aug 20 09:41:55 box sshd[2210]: Accepted publickey for dev
Aug 20 10:02:11 box nginx[813]: 502 upstream timed out

stage.label: the journal
stage.sub: is a database, not a text file

cmdJournalctl.verdictSub: every flag narrows the set, and they stack

scenes.narration: When a piece of hardware starts to fail, the kernel notices it long before anything gets written down in a log file anywhere. The command is D mesg, and D mesg prints that buffer, which isn't a log file at all. D mesg's fixed in size and it's a ring, which means new messages come in one end and the oldest are pushed off the other and lost. Dash T makes timestamps readable; by default they're seconds since boot. Now why you care: a disk starting to fail, a cable going bad, memory throwing errors, all of it appears here first, long before anything writes it to a log file. So check it early. On a busy machine that buffer wraps, and the message that explained everything is simply gone. Dmesg dash T piped into tail is worth running whenever a machine behaves strangely.

cmdDmesg.headline: dmesg is a [ring buffer]
cmdDmesg.verdictSub: because the kernel notices long before anything writes a log

quiz.question: Service works, dies after reboot. Missed what?

scenes.narration: Drawer nine runs without you. Tar and gzip package it. Cron schedules it. System C T L and journal C T L supervise it. T mux keeps it alive while you sleep.
Drawer ten. What to do when you're stuck, which is why these exist.

The manual isn't one book, it's numbered sections, and knowing that changes how useful it is. Section one is user commands. Section five is file formats. Section eight is administration. The same word can appear on several of those shelves. So man passwd gives you the command that changes a password. But man five passwd gives you the format of the etc passwd file, a completely different page answering a completely different question. The number in brackets at the top of any page tells you which one you're reading. If a manual page seems to be answering the wrong question, you're almost certainly on the wrong shelf. When a manual page seems to answer the wrong question, check the section number first.

cmdMan.headline: man passwd and man [5] passwd differ

stage.label: the number in brackets
stage.sub: tells you which you are reading

cmdMan.verdictSub: which is why man passwd sometimes seems to answer the wrong question

scenes.narration: Here's the situation the manual normally fails at. You know exactly what you want to do, but you don't know what the command is called, and man needs a name you don't have. Apropos solves it, because it searches the one-line descriptions of every manual page rather than their names. So ask it about disk usage and back come D U, which estimates file space usage, D F, which reports filesystem space, and N C D U, the interactive one. Three tools, from three different sections, found by describing the job. Man dash K is the identical command with a shorter name. Apropos answers the question you actually have, which is usually what was that thing called. Apropos is the command to remember for the days you've forgotten every other one.

cmdApropos.headline: apropos searches [descriptions]

stage.label: ncdu
stage.sub: disk usage analyzer with an interface

cmdApropos.verdict: It is the answer to what was that called
cmdApropos.verdictSub: which is the question you actually have most of the time

scenes.narration: The manual is complete, and completeness isn't always what you need at four in the afternoon. The page for tar runs to twelve hundred and forty one lines. T L D R's thorough and entirely correct. T L D R, which stands for too long, didn't read, gives you eight lines instead: the handful of things people actually do with the command, written as examples you can copy. And what you wanted was almost certainly one of them. These aren't competitors. The manual is the reference you go to when the detail genuinely matters and you need to be sure. T L D R is the reminder you want when you've done this before and simply can't recall the flag order. Keep both. Install tldr today. T L D R'll save you the twelve hundred lines you didn't want to read. The manual settles arguments; tldr just gets you back to work.

cmdTldr.headline: tldr gives you the [normal] usage

stage.label: what you wanted
stage.sub: was almost certainly one of them

cmdTldr.verdict: You need both, at different moments
cmdTldr.verdictSub: one is a reference, the other is a reminder

scenes.narration: There are three kinds of documentation and this is the third. The manual is written by the people who wrote the tool. T L D R is written by the community. Cheat is written by you. Dash E opens your own sheet for a command, and whatever flag you keep forgetting gets written down once, then recalled later exactly as you left it. That matters more than it sounds, because your notes can hold the details no general documentation ever will: your server names, your paths, the exact R sync incantation your deployment needs. Write it down the second time you look something up, because there's always a third time and you'll not remember then either. Your own notes, written once, beat re-reading somebody else's documentation three times.

cmdCheat.headline: cheat stores [your own] notes

stage.label: your notes
stage.sub: for your setup, with your paths

cmdCheat.verdict: Write it down the second time
cmdCheat.verdictSub: because there is always a third time, and you will not remember then either

scenes.narration: A graphics card is installed, the machine boots perfectly well, and yet absolutely nothing on the system appears to be using the thing at all. L S P C I dash K is where you find out why, because L S P C I lists hardware on the bus with the driver bound to each piece. The device is present, so the bus can see it. A kernel driver is in use, here i nine one five. Both of those need to be true. When that driver line is missing entirely, the hardware is present and completely unusable, and nothing will tell you: no error, no warning, it simply isn't used. That's a missing driver, not broken hardware, which is where an evening disappears. Present isn't working. Present and working are two different states, and lspci dash K is what tells them apart. Check the driver line before blaming the card, because that's where the evening goes.

cmdLspci.headline: lspci shows the [driver] too

steps.label: lspci -k
steps.text: 00:02.0 VGA  Kernel driver in use: i915

stage.label: no driver line at all
stage.sub: and it is present but useless

stage.label: which is where an evening goes

cmdLspci.verdict: Present is not the same as working
cmdLspci.verdictSub: and it is the second line, not the first, that tells you which

scenes.narration: Everything you plug in over U S B forms a physical tree, whether or not you ever picture it that way, and that shape explains a problem that otherwise makes no sense. L S U S B dash T draws the tree. At the top sits bus one, the root hub on the motherboard. Into one port you've plugged an external hub, and hanging off it are a keyboard and an external drive. Here's what which tells you. Those two share one link back to the machine. The keyboard needs almost none of it; the drive would use all of it. So when that drive runs slowly and nothing about the drive changed, the answer is in this tree. Move it to a port on the machine, which has a link of its own. Nothing was broken; it was sharing. Before you replace a slow drive, look at the tree and try a different port. USB bandwidth is shared per hub, so where you plug something in genuinely matters.

cmdLsusb.headline: lsusb shows the [tree]

stage.label: Bus 001
stage.sub: the root hub, on the motherboard

stage.label: a port on the machine
stage.sub: has a link of its own

cmdLsusb.verdictSub: which is why the answer is often to move one device, not to replace it
